# China, India and the prospects of a BRICS-led maritime order in the Indian Ocean Region

## ABSTRACT

This article employs geopolitical analysis to assess BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa) through a maritime perspective, with a specific focus on the Indian Ocean Region (IOR), and the possibility of the expanded BRICS (now including Iran, Egypt, Ethiopia, the United Arab Emirates and Indonesia) to serve as a mediating influence in the geopolitical rivalry and tensions that exist between China and India. As a bloc of emerging powers, many with maritime interests in the IOR, BRICS provides a possible avenue for collaboration and cooperation between China and India. The article explores new dimensions of BRICS as expanded and the prospects of a BRICS-led order in the IOR.

## Introduction

China and India are key emerging powers in Asia, with a relationship marked by both competition and cooperation. They are also both members of the BRICS (originally Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa) grouping, which aims for cooperation among members on many fronts. However, both countries’ reorientation towards the maritime domain, and their competition for influence and dominance in the Indian Ocean Region (IOR), have caused turbulence in relations, and also heightened maritime security concerns.

The Indian Ocean has become an arena of growing geopolitical competition between China and India. It is the third largest ocean, occupying an area roughly equal to Asia and Africa combined, connecting the continents of Asia, Africa and Europe. The IOR encompasses the Indian Ocean and land territory stretching from the Strait of Malacca in the east to the Mozambique Channel in the west, and includes the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal, the Gulf of Aden, the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, as well as 33 littoral countries with a total regional population of 2.9 billion. The IOR is critical for the world’s trade; nearly 90,000 ships pass through the region’s waters yearly, accounting for $7 trillion in total trade in 2022. Footnote 1 The area within the continental shorelines is also rich in natural resources, including hydrocarbons, minerals and living resources such as fish stock. Footnote 2 Within the region are several crucial ‘choke points’ through which goods, oil and energy traverse. These include the Six-degree Channel, the Eight/Nine-degree Channels, the Straits of Hormuz, the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, the Strait of Malacca, the Singapore Strait, the Sunda and Lombok Straits, the Mozambique Channel, and the Cape of Good Hope. Securing these channels and the trade going through them is critical. While traditionally the United States has provided security on the high seas, India and China are increasingly vying for influence in the IOR, which increases the friction between the two and thus the chance of conflict.

The great US naval strategist Admiral Alfred Thayer Mahan captured the geopolitical significance of the IOR well when he observed in 1890 in his work, The Influence of Sea Power Upon History 1660-1783: ‘Whoever controls the Indian Ocean dominates Asia. This ocean is the key to the seven seas. In the 21st century, the destiny of the world will be decided in its waters’. Footnote 3 

This fact makes it all the more compelling to consider the theatre for cooperation available to China and India in the BRICS grouping. This heterogeneous coalition, which expanded in 2024 to include Iran, Egypt, Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Footnote 4 first convened in 2009 and has since met annually to seek areas of cooperation. BRICS members have maritime interests and have demonstrated a desire to work together in the maritime domain. Footnote 5 BRICS thus provides an avenue for collaboration and cooperation between China and India. This study explores the prospects of a BRICS-led order in the IOR and ascertains how the group may help mediate the geopolitical differences between its competing Asian members.

The study sets out to highlight China and India’s geopolitical interests, concerns and rivalry in the Indian Ocean and proceeds to develop recommendations for their cooperation through BRICS. A brief overview of China and India in the IOR begins the discussion below. A geopolitical analysis of China and India in the IOR will follow respectively. BRICS as a platform for cooperation and coordination will be elaborated upon before the article explores the opportunities and challenges for Chinese/Indian collaboration under BRICS. Finally, before the conclusion, discussion will focus on the prospects of, and recommendations for, a BRICS-led order in the IOR.

## Maritime interests in the Indian Ocean Region

China and India as preeminent regional powers have at various times in history relied on land routes as well as the maritime front for the extension of their power. They had successfully established strategic political, economic, social and cultural links in Africa, Eurasia, the Mediterranean and Persia in what was referred to as the maritime silk route. Footnote 6 Their enormous wealth through trade and resources attracted various invaders over the centuries, eventually falling prey to imperial colonialism, which also relied upon the seas. Shedding over 200 years of colonial legacy, China and India have to varying extents revived their naval capabilities and power potential and have regained their ability to compete and exert influence in their maritime domains and beyond. However, their bilateral relationship is still dogged by suspicion and sensitivities about the safety and security of sea lanes, among other geopolitical concerns. Footnote 7 The growing Sino-India rivalry in the IOR resembles the ancient naval competition for markets, resources and military bases among industrialising imperial powers in history. Footnote 8 

China and India’s rivalry in the IOR has invited China’s other neighbouring states who share similar tense relations with Beijing into a comprehensive partnership with India, seeking to play a balancing role. India is a member of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (QUAD) with Australia, the US and Japan, with one stated intention being to challenge China’s influence in the region. Footnote 9 India’s strategy is to maintain its powerful naval presence in the IOR and prevent other regional powers from gaining ground in this strategic maritime region. Footnote 10 China has increased its presence in the IOR as well, deepening partnerships and creating a nexus of physical presence across South Asia. Footnote 11 Aware of its limits in terms of its inferior position relative to the US maritime power, and also aware of India’s strategic advantage in the IOR, China is expected to pursue a ‘harmonious seas’ approach, promoting maritime cooperation with littoral states while projecting its power. Footnote 12 Some observers argue that China’s refusal to recognise India’s claims to great power status or its special prerogatives in the IOR is a mistake, as should Beijing fail to enlist India as a partner to address some of its concerns in the IOR, it will find it difficult to make progress towards its own goals. Footnote 13 Mohan Malik, for instance, notes that ‘Beijing’s stance that the South China Sea is China’s sea, but the Indian Ocean cannot be treated as India’s ocean, draws New Delhi’s ire and derision’. Footnote 14 

India and China are both concerned about protecting their interests throughout the region and as they extend their reach and influence, they are bumping into each other. Robert Kaplan surmised in 2009 that a peaceful rise in great power aspirations and the quest for energy and security by the two rising powers would be managed largely by the US. Footnote 15 In 2018, Bruce Vaugh pointed to what he then termed a ‘pacifying role’ for the US as a balancing power, as well as to the interdependencies between China and India that should dampen their rivalry. Footnote 16 Currently, while the US looks more inward under President Donald Trump, India and China are engaging in cautious diplomacy and border agreements in attempts to rebuild trust and improve relations. Footnote 17 

China and India’s inland competition has already led to military engagements, if on a limited scale, most recently over disputed borders, and there are signs of maritime tensions in the strategic Indian Ocean. With both countries enlarging their naval military capabilities, the possibility for conflict grows, as their competition is increasingly characterised by hostility. Footnote 18 Despite their problems being structural, Maria Bastos argues that the two cannot sustain high-level strife in the region without endangering their own interests; Footnote 19 the fact that their geostrategic manoeuvres are influenced by energy and security concerns makes it likely that while they will remain adversaries, they are unlikely to become outright enemies. Instead, China and India have the opportunity to focus on securing this competition between adversaries via different multi-polar blocs in which they are members. Some go so far as to posit that ‘China and India hold the potential to create a serious counter-hegemonic order, by entering into competing trends, and not destructive ones’. Footnote 20 However, other scholars are pessimistic and argue that New Delhi’s perspective of Chinese policies – which is to encircle India – and Beijing’s view on India’s determination to limit China’s influence and power projection in the IOR far outweigh their mechanical statements of shared interests as partners in strengthening a multipolar world. Footnote 21 

India and China are re-evaluating their geopolitical interests in the IOR in a newly forming global order. Previous research has concentrated on their rivalry and antagonism in the IOR. This article explores the possibility of maritime cooperation in the context of an existing cooperative mechanism: the BRICS.

The maritime interests of BRICS countries can only become meaningfully addressed if it includes maritime security governance and cooperation in the Indian Ocean. A maritime BRICS has been under-explored, despite its importance to other bloc efforts to improve connectivity, trade and security, among others, as well as to the relations between these two major actors within the bloc. The article therefore endeavours to focus on the overlooked prospects of the BRICS as a mediating actor to defuse the geopolitical rivalry and maritime tensions between China and India in the IOR. Against this background, a geopolitical analysis of China and India in the IOR will highlight their geopolitical concerns and priorities. Theoretical approaches to geopolitics are used to assess a maritime BRICS and the prospects of a BRICS-led order in the IOR. The authors propose that BRICS as a cooperative platform can go beyond economic cooperation, facilitating cooperation in the maritime security domain to reduce friction between China and India in the IOR. The article’s major contribution lies in the exploration of new dimensions of BRICS, considering the role of maritime interests – especially in the IOR – as a determinant factor in a cohesive BRICS.
